why: An unverified race-committee contact pushes a same-day entry payment to a domain registered nine days ago, leaning on her sailing at Caldermere Quay.
A routine meeting notice from the association's long-established domain with no link, payment or credential request.
Delegate feedback from the forum's 2012 domain, pasted inline with no link, login or ask.
A prospect from an established domain confirming a call booked through her own booking page, with no link or request.
An unidentified sender asks for a call-back and a payroll yes/no before a deadline, so she should confirm who it is through a known channel first.
A courteous cold request for an introduction from an aged domain, with no link, money or credentials involved.
A sailmaker on a 2009 domain invoices a small, specific repair with bank details stated as unchanged and collection in person.
An unpaid trustee search from a decade-old firm domain linking to its own site, with a distant deadline and no payment or credential ask.
A registry notice from its long-standing domain that sends nothing by email and points her to the number on a prior registry letter.
A follow-up brief after an in-person lunch from an old domain, asking for no action and carrying no link.
A two-week-old domain asks her to register her work email and set a password on its 'data room', a credential-harvesting pattern.
An advance-fee 'release fee' for her speaker honorarium paid through a lookalike domain registered four days ago.
A ten-day-old domain sends a macro-enabled .docm and tells her to enable editing, a classic malware delivery.
An unsolicited SMS 'security alert' for her network profile pushes her to call an unknown number within two hours, a callback-phishing pattern.
A domain registered three weeks ago impersonates her alumni committee and uses scarcity to drive her to a personalised registration link.
A speaking invitation from the school's 2007 domain with no link or payment and a relaxed reply date.
A panel invitation from the podcast's established domain pointing to an event site set up weeks ago, with no login, payment or pressure.
An automated filing acknowledgement from the registry's long-standing domain with no link or action requested.
A domain registered eleven days ago asks her to sign in to 'verify' her charterholder record under a deadline threat, credential phishing.
A committee invitation from a domain she cannot tie to the forum asks for her address and phone, so she should confirm it with the forum through a known contact first.
A return invitation from the forum's 2012 domain linking to a months-old event site, with no login or payment and a distant deadline.
A twelve-day-old lookalike club domain asks for her membership number via a proxy-vote link under a short deadline.
A supplier says payment details have changed and are only in the attachment, a payment-diversion pattern she should confirm by phone with the caterer before paying or opening.
An informational fee notice from the registry's long-standing domain that states no action is required.
A 'new number, lost my contacts' opener that contradicts itself and name-drops the Trustees group to start a conversation from an unknown number.
A routine renewal from the club's 2008 domain with an unchanged account, a pay-at-the-bar option and a normal deadline.
A 'new number' friend asks for money through a payment link on a domain registered four days ago.
The podcast's producer from its established domain sends a .docx transcript for correction with no link, payment or login.
